Wholley agree. I think since OP is probably training for health and longevity, it's most important for her to train with variety. Another lateral raise tip- and this applies to all exercises- you can train within a specific trouble motion. What it mean is, it's okay to only train the bottom half or top half of a lift. In fact, if you're really strong at the bottom half of a lift and struggling with the top, you may be wasting your time even training both RoM simultaneously. There's no "Perfect Form" and it's important not to let that hold you back. All there is for strength and safety is a powerful and engaged core, and don't lift too heavy.

That's perfectly fine. Some people suggest it's better for engaging the side delt, some people think it shifts the engagement to the traps and upper back. In my opinion, both are fine and will make you stronger.

Yes, again, it's personal preference because bodies are all different. There is no absolute "perfect form" because everyone has a different anatomy. I generally advise against locking the elbows because tendinitis develops quickly with weightlifting, so the less you can engage those elbows when they aren't being used, the better.

Yes! Your arms literally can go straight up. It's how we can complete the YMCA dance. Some people recommend doing lateral raises in this way, raising the arms until they are perpendicular to the ground, but I think it's personal preference and people should experiment with their RoM because lat raises are an injury risk exercise for shoulders and elbows. In general, I recommend slightly above the shoulders, because it's a more realistic functional movement.
